# Ali Emre Özcan

## In one line
I'm a final-year computer engineering student at İTÜ and a part-time machine learning engineer at TAZI. My senior thesis asks whether a monitor that flags failed LLM-agent runs still works when the models and the environment drift.
The question underneath my work: how can a learned system tell that it has failed, or is about to? LLM agents under workload drift, RL policies off their training distribution.
Applying to PhD and master's programs for Fall 2027.

## Projects
- Monitoring LLM agents under drift [ml, agents, research] — Python, PyTorch Geometric, scikit-learn, vLLM, MCPMark (slug: thesis)
  An LLM agent can fail a task while its run looks ordinary. Can a monitor that learns only from successful tool-calling runs flag the failed ones, and does it keep working, without a flood of false alarms, when the model or the environment changes?
  My senior thesis at İTÜ, advised by Prof. Gülşen Cebiroğlu Eryiğit. Results so far are preliminary; the work is being prepared for a 2027 ML workshop, with a preprint and public code planned after that.
  An agent run is a sequence of tool calls. The monitor learns what normal, passing runs look like and flags runs that deviate; failed runs are used only to score it, never to train it. The data is 10,298 public MCPMark runs (5 MCP services, 127 tasks, 22 model configurations) and about 2,800 runs of my own with Qwen3-8B and gpt-oss-20b on İTÜ’s HPC. I compared a ladder of encodings: run length, counts, action n-grams, graphs of tool calls (sequence, data-flow and repeat edges), and text. A pre-registered result, negative twice: graph edges add no detection gain. A logistic regression over text and action types is the strongest detector so far. Drift comes in two ways: a new model family, or distractor files added to the environment that leave every correct answer unchanged. Training on several model families keeps false alarms near 5% when the model changes. Distractors push up to 57% of correct runs over a 5% threshold, and recalibrating on about 50 new normal runs brings it back down. The open problem is telling a shift that hurts the agent from one it merely meets: so far every drop in pass rate comes from tasks built so the agent runs into the distractors.
- Target-Aware Whole-Body Throwing [ml, research] — Python, MuJoCo, TD3, PPO, Unitree G1 (slug: throwing)
  Teach a Unitree G1 humanoid to hit targets at varying distances while walking, in simulation, without falling.
  The final TD3 policy landed 0.177 m from the target on average, hit 100% of targets within 0.5 m and never fell across a held-out target sweep.
  Built in July 2026 at the Audi Development Camp in Győr by a six-person, five-country team selected for the programme run by Széchenyi István University with Audi Hungaria. I was project manager and integration lead, and owned the reinforcement-learning controller. The task is staged curriculum learning: a fixed throw first, then throwing while walking, then a target that changes. Potential-based reward shaping kept each stage learnable. We benchmarked PPO against TD3 and adopted TD3 for its off-policy sample efficiency.

## Reading
- 2026-10 paper: GRADE: Graph Representation of LLM Agent Dependency and Execution — Zhao. One typed graph per agent run, execution and dependency together: the closest prior work to the trace graphs I tested in my thesis.
- 2026-09 paper: WebGuard: Building a Generalizable Guardrail for Web Agents — Zheng et al.. Judges whether a web agent’s next action is risky before it runs; my thesis asks whether a run went wrong after the fact, from its trace.
- 2026-08 paper: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools — Schick et al.. Teaching a model when to call a tool. My thesis starts from the runs where that call goes wrong.
- 2026-07 paper: ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs — Qian et al.. Rewards built around correct tool calls, and a useful map of the ways a tool call can go wrong.
- 2026-06 paper: Addressing Function Approximation Error in Actor-Critic Methods — Fujimoto, van Hoof & Meger. TD3. Why we picked it over PPO for the sample efficiency of the G1 throwing controller.
- 2026-05 paper: Policy Invariance Under Reward Transformations: Theory and Application to Reward Shaping — Ng, Harada & Russell. Potential-based shaping: how our staged curriculum could shape rewards without changing the optimal policy.
- 2026-04 paper: BLoB: Bayesian Low-Rank Adaptation by Backpropagation for Large Language Models — Wang et al.. Calibrated uncertainty for fine-tuned LLMs: the direction I want to bring into keeping a failure detector honest under drift.
- 2026-03 paper: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models — Yao et al.. The reason, act, observe loop that produces the traces my thesis monitors.
- 2026-02 paper: Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift — Ovadia et al.. Uncertainty degrades under dataset shift while the model stays confident: the failure mode I test my detector against.
- 2025-12 paper: A Baseline for Detecting Misclassified and Out-of-Distribution Examples in Neural Networks — Hendrycks & Gimpel. The baseline for flagging inputs a model has not seen before; my thesis applies the same idea to agent runs.
- 2025-10 paper: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks — Kipf & Welling. Where graph encoders start. My thesis tested whether graph structure helps on agent traces; so far it does not.
